chapter_theme: The dread of begging (இரவச்சம்): a person of worth would rather go hungry and poor than ask, even of willing givers, because the mind melts at the thought of asking and a refusal kills. The only givers the chapter allows are those who welcome one in, and the last quatrain turns to the help owed to an old friend.
structure_note: 301, 303 and 304 say whom the worthy will not follow or approach. 302, 306 and 309 weigh hunger and poverty against begging and find begging worse. 305, 307 and 308 describe what begging feels like: shame, scorn, and death at a refusal. 310 closes on the giver's side, with the claim of old friendship.

301.reading: Would people of clear understanding follow after the self-deluded rich, who tell themselves that the poor live only through them and have no means of their own?
301.nuance: The fault named is the patron's self-importance, not his stinginess. Mudaliar glosses தம்மை மருண்ட as being dazed by one's own estimate of oneself.

302.reading: Since dying and being born again takes no longer than opening the eyes and blinking, is it wrong for a man to go hungry without doing anything blameworthy rather than eat his fill by doing what degrades him?
302.nuance: The argument rests on the shortness of a life: a full stomach bought with disgrace feeds a body that will be gone in a blink. Mudaliar gives three ways to take the eye image, one of them sleeping and waking, and cites Kural 339 for it.

303.reading: Some, leaning on their poverty, will dare to beg and take the mean road, but the worthy go before no one except those who embrace them and say 'come in, eat'.
303.nuance: Mudaliar reads முகம் புகுதல் as putting up with a patron's frown, and Shanmuganar as showing one's own face to a patron. Either way, the only giver the worthy approach is one who receives them as a guest.

304.reading: Though fortune leaves him and the gods turn against him, the man of worth keeps his mind on his own high standing and never stands with bowed neck behind fools who hoard their wealth.
304.nuance: திரு and தெய்வம் are the two supports a person might count on, and the verse takes both away before asking for steadiness. The stance is independence from fortune, not defiance of it. Mudaliar takes உருத்த மனம் as a mind roused with energy.

305.reading: Real living is to live without asking even of those dear as one's eyes, whose love is firm and who hold nothing back; the heart melts at the mere thought of begging, so what must the asker feel at the moment of taking?
305.nuance: The last line moves from the giver to what the receiver feels while taking. Mudaliar reads கொள்வார் குறிப்பு as the taker's state of mind; Shanmuganar names it as shame.

306.reading: When poverty can be ended by asking of oneself, 'let pain come, let pleasures go', why should anyone, with a mind racked by desire and eyes sunk, go begging of strangers?
306.nuance: Mudaliar divides தானிரப்ப two ways: தான் நிரப்ப, filling oneself with contentment, or தான் இரப்ப, begging of oneself. Pope takes the second and Shanmuganar the first. On either reading the cure for poverty is inward: consenting to hardship removes the want that drives begging.

307.reading: Though new people are born into this world every day, the man who does not scorn beggars has never been born, lord of the hill country where waterfalls carry gold down every slope.
307.nuance: Mudaliar gives two reasons for the overstatement: such a man reaches the good state and is not born again, or he simply cannot be found. The first plays on பிறக்கலான் ('is not born').

308.reading: With want wasting his body outside and his good sense put away inside, a man goes to another and says 'give to me'; if he is refused, will he not die on the spot?
308.nuance: Two losses come before the refusal: the body already worn down by want, and the understanding set aside so that asking is possible at all. Shanmuganar adds that the death would come from shame.

309.reading: It is proper to attach oneself to another and serve him with respect, but is the slow road of poverty more painful than losing one's dignity and saying 'won't you do something for me?'
309.nuance: Both commentators allow dependence on a patron, with deference, and forbid only the words of asking, so the line is drawn in speech. Mudaliar derives பைய from பை (suffering); Shanmuganar takes it as 'slowly'. Pope's 'to the hermitage' is his own addition.

310.reading: Where old acquaintance has grown into affection, one should do whatever help that intimacy calls for; if the claim of intimacy is not borne, it becomes a fire banked in the heart that burns without end.
310.nuance: Whose heart burns is not settled. Shanmuganar says it is the old friend who came to ask and was turned away. Pope reverses the roles: help is offered, and the needy friend who cannot bear to accept it burns. Mudaliar says only that the one asked fails to give the fitting help.

links.note: Both ask why a person of worth should stand behind those who look down on him. 966 counts the loss in renown and in heaven; 301 in clear understanding.

656 forbids deeds the wise condemn even to relieve one's mother's hunger. 302 makes the same choice for one's own hunger, and grounds it in the shortness of life rather than in the judgement of the wise.

Both make death and rebirth as brief as an ordinary act of the eyes, and Mudaliar cites 339 here. The Kural uses the image to show impermanence; 302 uses it to make blameless hunger the cheaper choice.
1053 finds a beauty even in asking before unconcealing givers who know their duty. 303 narrows this further: the worthy approach only givers who first welcome them in, so asking becomes hospitality.
963 asks for dignity when circumstances shrink; 304 shows it, with fortune and the gods both gone and the worthy still refusing to bow to the hoarding rich.
The first half restates 1061: not asking even of givers dear as one's eyes, who give without holding back, is far better. Both use the same phrase, கண்ணன்னார்.
Both have the heart melt (உள்ளம் உருகும்) at the thought of begging. 1069 goes on to the one who refuses; 305 to the beggar at the moment of taking.

Both reject begging as a cure for poverty. In Parimelazhagar's reading the Kural's alternative is effort; 306's is to want less and consent to hardship. They differ on the remedy, not on the refusal, and the difference shows the Naladiyar's turn toward renunciation.

1057 speaks of beggars rejoicing when they meet givers who give without scorn, which assumes such givers exist. 307 says the man who does not scorn beggars has never been born. The conflict holds only if 307 is taken literally; Mudaliar's explanations treat it as overstatement or wordplay.
In both, the asker's life goes out at the word of refusal. 1070 turns the point against the refuser; 308 stays with the asker.
1066 finds nothing more degrading to the tongue than asking, even for water for a cow. 309 also places the disgrace in the spoken request rather than in dependence.
803 asks what use old friendship is if a friend's liberties aren't accepted as one's own. On Shanmuganar's reading, 310 shows the cost of that failure to the friend who relied on it.
